source_refs.note: Topic 19.7 (PDF 47-50). The book announces four types of reaction but describes seven; all seven are given. The propene + HBr product is corrected to 2-bromopropane, matching Quick Check 19.6.

blocks.text: Organic reactions are easier to understand with three basic ideas: a covalent bond can break in two ways (homolytic and heterolytic); there are three types of reagent (free radicals, electrophiles and nucleophiles); and reactions fall into a few general types.

items: Homolytic fission (homolysis) happens when a non-polar bond breaks: the two shared electrons are shared out equally, one to each atom, e.g. Cl-Cl -> Cl. + .Cl and H3C-H -> .CH3 + H. (the dot is the unpaired electron). Atoms or groups with unpaired electrons are free radicals; they are reactive intermediates because the unpaired electron tends to pair up.
Heterolytic fission (heterolysis) happens when a polar bond breaks: one atom keeps both electrons and becomes negative, while the other is left one electron short and becomes positive.

blocks.alt: Left: Cl-Cl with two half-headed arrows from the bond to each Cl, giving two Cl atoms each with one unpaired electron. Right: (CH3)3C-Cl, with C delta+ and Cl delta-, and a curly arrow from the bond to Cl, giving the carbocation (CH3)3C+ and Cl-.
blocks.caption: Homolytic and heterolytic fission (original diagram after the book's examples).
blocks.long_description: In homolysis each atom takes one electron of the bonding pair, shown by half-headed (fish-hook) arrows, and two free radicals form. In heterolysis the more electronegative atom takes both electrons, shown by one full curly arrow, giving a positive and a negative ion.

items: A carbocation is a species with a positively charged carbon atom. It forms when carbon is bonded to a more electronegative atom such as O, N, S or Cl, e.g. (CH3)3C-Cl -> (CH3)3C+ + Cl-.
A carbanion, with a negatively charged carbon, forms when carbon is bonded to a less electronegative metal atom such as Li, Mg or Cd.

blocks.text: A reaction can be seen as the attack of one species on another: the attacking species is the reagent and the species attacked is the substrate.

blocks.caption: Types of reagent
rows: Free radical
an atom or group with an unpaired electron
Cl., H., .CH3, CH3COO.
Electrophile (electron lover)
accepts a pair of electrons to form a new bond; a positive ion (including carbocations) or a neutral molecule
CH3+, H+, Br+, NO2+, SO3, BF3
Nucleophile (nucleus lover)
donates a pair of electrons to form a new bond; a negative ion (including carbanions) or a neutral molecule with a lone pair
CH3-, Br-, OH-, CN-, NH3, H2O, ROH

blocks.text: Electrophilic and nucleophilic sites are not limited to ions: in a polar molecule the partial charges create them. In CH3-OH the carbon is delta+ (electrophilic) and the oxygen delta- (nucleophilic); in CH3-Li the carbon is delta- (nucleophilic) and lithium delta+.

blocks.caption: Types of organic reaction with the book's examples
rows: Substitution
an atom or group in one molecule is replaced by another; two products may form
CH3CH2Br + KOH(aq) -> CH3CH2OH + KBr
Addition
two reactants give a single product
CH2=CH2 + H2 -> CH3-CH3 (Ni, 200-300 C); CH3CH=CH2 + HBr -> CH3CHBrCH3
Elimination
atoms or groups are removed from two neighbouring atoms to form a multiple bond; the reverse of addition
CH3CH2Br + KOH (in alcohol) -> CH2=CH2 + KBr + H2O
Hydrolysis
a compound is split by reaction with water, often helped by H+ or OH-
CH3COOCH2CH3 + H2O -> CH3COOH + CH3CH2OH (H+)
Condensation
two molecules join into a bigger one, with or without loss of a small molecule such as H2O, NH3 or HCl
CH3COCH3 + H2N-OH -> (CH3)2C=N-OH + H2O (propanone oxime)
Oxidation
loss of electrons, gain of oxygen, loss of hydrogen, more C-O bonds or a higher oxidation state of carbon
CH3CH=CH2 with O3 then Zn/H2O -> CH3CHO + HCHO
Reduction
gain of electrons, loss of oxygen, gain of hydrogen, fewer C-O bonds or a lower oxidation state of carbon
CH2=CH2 + H2 -> CH3-CH3 (Ni)
